title: Introduction to Signal Processing, Second Edition
topics: Chapter 24, Exponential Moving Average Filters (physical PDF pp. 1183-1231; printed pp. 1160-1208): mean tracking, forecasting, polynomial smoothing, reduced lag, and initialization.
Sec. 24.1: sample means, sliding-window averages, exact and steady-state EMA, predictor/corrector form, estimator variance, noise-reduction ratio, effective memory, lag, and initialization.
Sec. 24.2: EMA forecasting, innovations, ARIMA(0,1,1) interpretation, and constant-level state-space/Kalman models.
Secs. 24.3-24.4: exponentially weighted and FIR local-polynomial least squares, level/slope/acceleration estimates, predictive FIR filters, moment constraints, and minimum-norm designs.
Secs. 24.5-24.6: exact recursive high-order exponential smoothing, RLS-like gain and covariance recursions, steady-state limits, and multiple-EMA realizations.
Sec. 24.7: choosing smoothing parameters by equivalent FIR length, noise-reduction ratio, MSE, MAE, and MAPE criteria.
Secs. 24.8-24.11: single/double/triple EMA, Tukey twicing, Kaiser-Hamming filter sharpening, zero-lag tradeoffs, and general local level/slope/acceleration filters.
Secs. 24.12-24.13: polynomial-to-cascade basis transformations, practical initialization, Holt level/trend smoothing, and Holt-Winters seasonal extension.
Sec. 24.14: twelve derivation and computer-experiment problems on moments, lag, sharpening, predictive FIR filters, and Butterworth lag.
Chapter 25, Filtering Methods in Financial Markets (physical PDF pp. 1232-1293; printed pp. 1209-1270): DSP interpretations of technical indicators and portfolio optimization.
Secs. 25.1-25.2: technical analysis; SMA, WMA, TMA, EMA, and integrated linear-regression-slope filters; smoothing-versus-lag tradeoffs.
Sec. 25.3: predictive moving averages, local level/slope indicators, time-series forecasts, and minimum-noise filters with prescribed lag.
Secs. 25.4-25.6: single/double/triple EMA indicators, rolling linear regression and R-squared significance, standard errors, and initialization schemes.
Sec. 25.7: first- through higher-order Butterworth moving averages designed by the bilinear transform, with explicit lag formulas.
Sec. 25.8: reduced-lag constructions including twicing, generalized DEMA, T3, Kaiser-Hamming sharpening, Hull moving averages, and zero-lag EMA.
Secs. 25.9-25.10: nonlinear zigzag swing-point extraction and L0-regularized piecewise-linear or piecewise-constant trend indicators.
Sec. 25.11: Bollinger and standard-error bands, projection bands, Donchian channels, fixed-width/Keltner/STARC bands, average true range, and parabolic stop-and-reverse.
Secs. 25.12-25.13: RSI, CMO, VHF, directional movement, momentum, MACD, stochastic and volume indicators, TRIX, variable-length EMA, and a MATLAB function catalog.

Sec. 25.14: Markowitz mean-variance portfolios, efficient frontier, risk aversion, two-fund theorem, short-sale constraints, capital asset line, Sharpe ratio, CAPM, and multi-constraint quadratic optimization.
Chapter 26, Whittaker-Henderson Smoothing (physical PDF pp. 1294-1341; printed pp. 1271-1318): global trend extraction, regularization, sparse modeling, and inverse problems.
Secs. 26.1-26.2: continuous smoothing splines, discrete Whittaker-Henderson smoothing, difference penalties, sparse banded matrices, weighted observations, and GCV parameter selection.
Secs. 26.3-26.5: equivalent two-sided regularization filters, complementary residual filters, Hodrick-Prescott macroeconomic filtering, poles, and double-sided impulse responses.
Sec. 26.6: Tikhonov regularization and ridge regression for deconvolution, conditioning, basis expansions, reproducing kernels, and kernel machines.
Sec. 26.7: sparse Whittaker-Henderson smoothing via Lp penalties and iterative reweighted least squares.
Sec. 26.8: computer experiments on total variation, piecewise local trends, global-temperature anomalies, and U.S. GDP.
Sec. 26.9: LASSO/basis-pursuit denoising, L0/L1/L2 regularization, IRLS, sparse spike deconvolution, and underdetermined sparse recovery.
Sec. 26.10: problems on Whittaker-Henderson pole factorizations, Hodrick-Prescott parameters, and regularized deconvolution.
Chapter 27, Periodic Signal Extraction (physical PDF pp. 1342-1398; printed pp. 1319-1375): comb/notch filtering and seasonal decomposition.
Secs. 27.1-27.2: periodic signal-plus-trend-plus-noise models, harmonic DFT representation, integer-period comb/notch filters, frequency scaling, bandwidth, NRR, and circular-buffer realization.
Sec. 27.3: noninteger-period comb/notch filters using constrained least-squares fractional-delay FIR approximations.
Sec. 27.4: parallel peak-filter combs and cascaded notch filters as an alternative to fractional-delay designs.
Sec. 27.5: signal averaging as comb filtering and its SNR improvement for repeated signals.
Secs. 27.6-27.7: ideal trend/seasonal/irregular extraction filters and classical additive or multiplicative seasonal decomposition.
Sec. 27.8: seasonal moving-average filters, upsampled comb filters, and Whittaker-Henderson/Kaiser decomposition.
Sec. 27.9: the Census X-11/X-12 filtering sequence using 2x12 trend, 3x3/3x5 comb, and Henderson filters.
Sec. 27.10: Musgrave asymmetric minimum-revision end filters for finite time-series endpoints.
Secs. 27.11-27.12: simultaneous seasonal Whittaker-Henderson trend/seasonal estimation, sparse L1 version, frequency responses, and Wiener/state-space interpretation.
Sec. 27.13: four problems on periodic DFT identities, sampling constraints, power-complementary comb/notch filters, and seasonal WH algebra.
Chapter 28, Neural Networks (physical PDF pp. 1399-1411; printed pp. 1376-1388): a compact introduction to feedforward networks and backpropagation.
Secs. 28.1-28.2: multilayer feedforward architecture, affine connections, common activation functions, squared-error training, gradient descent, and pattern versus epoch updates.
Sec. 28.3: matrix backpropagation, layer error vectors, outer-product weight updates, momentum smoothing, and one-/two-hidden-layer algorithms.
Sec. 28.4: 3-bit parity with 3:3:2 and 3:3:2:2 networks and nonlinear autoregressive prediction of the sunspot series with a 4:4:1 network.
Chapter 29, Appendices (physical PDF pp. 1412-1455; printed pp. 1389-1432): random-number generation, prolate spheroidal wave functions, and toolbox location.
Appendix A.1: linear congruential uniform generators, overflow-safe Schrage arithmetic, interval transformations, and approximate Gaussian generation.
Appendix A.2: low-frequency noise by hold, linear, and higher-order interpolation with polyphase implementations.
Appendix A.3-A.4: Voss-style 1/f or pink-noise generation, theoretical PSD, periodogram tests, and eight implementation exercises.
Appendix B.1-B.3: PSWF definitions, sinc-kernel and finite Fourier eigenproblems, Shannon number, transforms, dual orthogonality, and completeness.
Appendix B.4-B.6: ill-conditioned signal restoration, spectral cutoff/Tikhonov regularization, bandlimited extrapolation, sinc/PSWF/Bessel bases, and optimum energy concentration.
Appendix B.7: tridiagonal eigenvalue computation of PSWFs and numerical verification of identities, delta approximations, and superoscillations.
Appendix C, References, and Index (physical PDF pp. 1455-1540; printed pp. 1432-1517): toolbox download pointer, 1437-item bibliography, and subject/function index.
key_results: Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1184-1188; printed pp. 1161-1165): the steady EMA update a_n=lambda a_(n-1)+(1-lambda)y_n is a predictor/corrector whose constant gain retains the ability to track changing means, unlike the running mean's gain 1/(n+1), which vanishes.

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1186-1188; printed pp. 1163-1165): for white observation noise, EMA NRR is (1-lambda)/(1+lambda), effective lag is lambda/(1-lambda), and matching both to an N-point SMA gives lambda=(N-1)/(N+1).

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1187-1188; printed pp. 1164-1165): for any unity-DC-gain filter, effective lag is sum_n n h_n, equivalently minus H'(1)/H(1) and the group delay at DC; smaller variance necessarily trades against slower response.

Sec. 24.2 (physical PDF pp. 1192-1193; printed pp. 1169-1170): EMA is the optimal one-step predictor for an IMA(1,1), or ARIMA(0,1,1), process; it is also the steady Kalman predictor for a random-walk state observed in white noise, with q=sigma_w^2/sigma_v^2=alpha^2/(1-alpha).

Secs. 24.3-24.4 (physical PDF pp. 1193-1198; printed pp. 1170-1175): weighted local-polynomial smoothing solves c=(S^TWS)^(-1)S^TWy; estimates at offset tau are linear filters whose moments exactly reproduce every polynomial of degree at most d.

Sec. 24.4 (physical PDF pp. 1196-1198; printed pp. 1173-1175): the order-1 predictive FIR filter is the minimum-NRR length-N filter constrained to unity DC gain and lag -tau; tau=0 yields local level, its derivative channel yields local slope, and tau=1 gives the next-sample forecast.

Secs. 24.5-24.6 (physical PDF pp. 1198-1209; printed pp. 1175-1186): high-order EMA admits an exact RLS-like recursion for polynomial state, gain, and inverse covariance; its large-time limit becomes a fixed-gain state-space smoother realizable by a cascade of identical first-order EMAs.

Secs. 24.8-24.10 (physical PDF pp. 1214-1219; printed pp. 1191-1196): twicing H into 2H-H^2 cancels first-order passband error and always produces zero DC lag; repeated residual correction gives 1-(1-H)^(d+1), while general Kaiser-Hamming sharpening can improve both passband and stopband orders.

Sec. 24.10 (physical PDF pp. 1217-1219; printed pp. 1194-1196): zero lag in a causal smoother requires negative impulse-response coefficients and commonly creates a passband peak just above DC; delay reduction is therefore not free.

Secs. 24.11-24.13 (physical PDF pp. 1219-1227; printed pp. 1196-1204): cascaded outputs of any unity-gain lowpass filter can be linearly combined into local level, slope, and acceleration estimates using its first two moments; Holt generalizes the level/slope gains independently, and Holt-Winters adds a D-period seasonal state.

Sec. 25.2 (physical PDF pp. 1233-1235; printed pp. 1210-1212): SMA, WMA, TMA, EMA, and ILRS filters are compared by the same two invariants, NRR=sum h_n^2 and lag=sum n h_n; increasing span reduces noise but increases decision delay.

Sec. 25.3 (physical PDF pp. 1235-1237; printed pp. 1212-1214): the predictive moving average h_tau minimizes NRR subject to unity gain and lag -tau; ordinary SMA and WMA emerge as tau=-(N-1)/2 and tau=-(N-1)/3 special cases.

Sec. 25.5 (physical PDF pp. 1240-1245; printed pp. 1217-1222): rolling least-squares line fits are exactly the local-level and local-slope FIR indicators; R-squared measures linear-fit strength, while residual variance gives explicit standard errors for level and slope.

Sec. 25.7 (physical PDF pp. 1251-1254; printed pp. 1228-1231): an Mth-order Butterworth moving average has squared response 1/[1+(tan(omega/2)/Omega_0)^(2M)], zeros at Nyquist, and lag 1/[2 Omega_0 sin(pi/(2M))], approximately MN/pi^2 for common M,N.

Sec. 25.8 (physical PDF pp. 1254-1260; printed pp. 1231-1237): a general combination H1[(1+v)H2-vH3] has lag n1+(1+v)n2-vn3, unifying DEMA/GDEMA, filter sharpening, HMA, and ZEMA and allowing a chosen reduced lag.

Secs. 25.9-25.10 (physical PDF pp. 1260-1264; printed pp. 1237-1241): zigzag filtering retains swing extrema exceeding a chosen percentage; L0 trend filtering instead minimizes squared data error plus the cardinality of an s-difference, producing nearly piecewise-constant trends for s=1 and piecewise-linear trends for s=2.

Sec. 25.11 (physical PDF pp. 1265-1274; printed pp. 1242-1251): volatility bands differ chiefly in their center and width estimators; parabolic SAR is a time-varying EMA of the current trend's extreme price whose gain increases on new extremes and resets when price crosses the stop.

Sec. 25.14 (physical PDF pp. 1282-1293; printed pp. 1259-1270): Markowitz portfolio selection is a linearly constrained quadratic minimization; its risk-return efficient frontier is parabolic, adding a risk-free asset creates a tangent capital asset line whose slope is the maximum Sharpe ratio, and CAPM makes excess return proportional to beta.

Secs. 26.1-26.2 (physical PDF pp. 1294-1299; printed pp. 1271-1276): smoothing splines balance weighted interpolation error against integrated derivative energy; the equally spaced Whittaker-Henderson analogue minimizes ||y-x||_W^2+lambda||D_s x||_2^2 and has solution x=(W+lambda D_s^T D_s)^(-1)Wy.

Sec. 26.2 (physical PDF pp. 1297-1299; printed pp. 1274-1276): D_s^T D_s is sparse and banded with width 2s+1, making global smoothing efficient; GCV provides an automatic lambda criterion but often undersmooths and must be checked visually or against domain constraints.

Sec. 26.3 (physical PDF pp. 1300-1302; printed pp. 1277-1279): the infinite-record WH smoother has H(omega)=1/[1+lambda|D(omega)|^2]; for s differences, H=1/[1+lambda|2sin(omega/2)|^(2s)] and the complementary residual filter is 1-H.

Sec. 26.4 (physical PDF pp. 1302-1305; printed pp. 1279-1282): the s=2 Hodrick-Prescott smoother with lambda=1600 on quarterly data has an approximately 32-quarter, -3.065 dB cutoff; preserving that cutoff requires rescaling lambda when sampling period or difference order changes.

Sec. 26.5 (physical PDF pp. 1305-1306; printed pp. 1282-1283): the WH transfer function has s reciprocal pole pairs; choosing the s inside-unit-circle poles yields a stable, real, symmetric, double-sided impulse response that decays exponentially away from time zero.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF pp. 1306-1311; printed pp. 1283-1288): Tikhonov deconvolution solves x=(F^TF+lambda D^TD)^(-1)F^Ty; positive lambda reduces condition number and noise amplification but introduces bias and smoothing.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF pp. 1308-1311; printed pp. 1285-1288): a regularized basis expansion can be rewritten entirely through kernel values K(x,x'), yielding the representer form f(x)=sum_n K(x,x_n)a_n with a=(lambda I+K)^(-1)y.

Secs. 26.7 and 26.9 (physical PDF pp. 1312-1314 and 1326-1332; printed pp. 1289-1291 and 1303-1309): replacing an L2 difference penalty by L1 or L0 promotes sparse derivatives; IRLS approximates |x|^p with a solution-dependent weighted quadratic and repeatedly solves sparse regularized least-squares systems.

Sec. 26.9 (physical PDF pp. 1330-1332; printed pp. 1307-1309): L1 regularization is convex and often recovers the L0-sparsest solution or a close approximation; L0 is more directly sparse but nonconvex and generally intractable without approximations such as IRLS.

Sec. 27.2 (physical PDF pp. 1343-1347; printed pp. 1320-1324): a D-period signal consists of D discrete harmonics; substituting z by z^D maps a prototype lowpass into a comb and a highpass into a notch filter with peaks or zeros at 2pi k/D.

Sec. 27.2 (physical PDF pp. 1345-1347; printed pp. 1322-1324): the first-order IIR comb/notch pair is both complementary and power-complementary; tan(D Delta omega/4)=(1-a)/(1+a) controls 3-dB width, while comb NRR=(1-a)/2.

Sec. 27.3 (physical PDF pp. 1349-1353; printed pp. 1326-1330): when D is noninteger, z^-D can be split into an integer delay and a constrained least-squares FIR fractional delay forced to match exp(-j omega_k d) exactly at every retained harmonic.

Sec. 27.5 (physical PDF pp. 1360-1366; printed pp. 1337-1343): averaging K synchronized repetitions is a comb-filter operation; coherent periodic components add while independent noise power averages down, improving SNR in proportion to K.

Secs. 27.6-27.7 (physical PDF pp. 1365-1374; printed pp. 1342-1351): trend, seasonal, and irregular extraction filters can be designed as complementary paths whose transfer functions sum to one; classical decomposition uses a centered 1xD or 2xD trend average followed by D-period signal averaging of the residual.

Sec. 27.9 (physical PDF pp. 1381-1385; printed pp. 1358-1362): X-11 refines classical decomposition through twelve staged applications of 2x12 trend, 3x3/3x5 seasonal comb, and Henderson smoothers; its effective trend, seasonal, and irregular filters remain complementary.

Sec. 27.10 (physical PDF pp. 1385-1391; printed pp. 1362-1368): Musgrave endpoint filters minimize expected revision error between a final symmetric estimate and the current asymmetric estimate, trading coefficient deviation against assumed local trend slope.

Sec. 27.11 (physical PDF pp. 1391-1393; printed pp. 1368-1370): seasonal WH jointly minimizes data error, trend-difference energy, and D-sample seasonal sums; the resulting sparse banded system estimates trend and seasonal components simultaneously in O(N) work.

Sec. 27.12 (physical PDF pp. 1393-1397; printed pp. 1370-1374): the joint seasonal-WH trend and seasonal frequency responses are Wiener-optimal for a model with white observation, trend-innovation, and seasonal-sum noises; lambda and alpha equal corresponding noise-variance ratios.

Secs. 28.2-28.3 (physical PDF pp. 1400-1405; printed pp. 1377-1382): a feedforward layer applies u=W x+b then an elementwise activation; backpropagation propagates error by transposed weight matrices and activation derivatives and updates each W by an error/input outer product.

Sec. 28.2 (physical PDF pp. 1401-1402; printed pp. 1378-1379): sufficiently small negative-gradient updates decrease the squared-error objective to first order, but the nonlinear objective can contain multiple local minima and is sensitive to initialization.

Sec. 28.3 (physical PDF pp. 1404-1405; printed pp. 1381-1382): pattern updating changes weights after each example, while epoch updating accumulates corrections across the training set; EMA smoothing of corrections supplies the classical momentum term.

Sec. 28.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 1408-1411; printed pp. 1385-1388): a nonlinear autoregressive network predicts y_n from p delayed samples; a meaningful diagnostic is that held-out prediction errors should be uncorrelated and have approximately delta autocorrelation.

Appendix A.1 (physical PDF pp. 1413-1417; printed pp. 1390-1394): the Park-Miller LCG uses a=16807 and m=2^31-1 for maximal period m-1; Schrage's quotient/remainder rearrangement performs the modular update without overflowing a signed 32-bit integer.
Appendix A.1 (physical PDF pp. 1416-1417; printed pp. 1393-1394): summing 12 independent U[0,1) values has mean 6 and variance 1, giving the practical Gaussian approximation x=m+s(sum u_i-6).

Appendix A.2 (physical PDF pp. 1417-1422; printed pp. 1394-1399): generating one random number every D samples and interpolating by hold or linear filters produces low-frequency noise; polyphase implementation evaluates only the active interpolation phase at the full output rate.

Appendix A.3 (physical PDF pp. 1422-1426; printed pp. 1399-1403): 1/f noise falls 3 dB per octave and has equal power in every octave; averaging held white-noise processes with periods 1,2,4,...,2^(B-1) approximates pink noise down to f_min=fs/2^B.

Appendix B.1 (physical PDF pp. 1430-1432; printed pp. 1407-1409): PSWFs are simultaneously bandlimited to [-omega_0,omega_0] and maximally concentrated on [-t_0,t_0]; eigenvalues remain near one for roughly the Shannon number N_c=2 omega_0 t_0/pi=FT, then fall rapidly.

Appendix B.2-B.3 (physical PDF pp. 1432-1436; printed pp. 1409-1413): PSWFs are eigenfunctions of both a sinc-kernel concentration operator and a finite Fourier transform, and form dual orthogonal complete bases for finite-interval square-integrable functions and globally bandlimited functions.

Appendix B.4 (physical PDF pp. 1436-1438; printed pp. 1413-1415): exact inversion of finite-aperture sinc blurring divides noise coefficients by eigenvalues tending to zero; truncating near the Shannon number or applying Tikhonov weights regularizes the restoration.

Appendix B.5-B.6 (physical PDF pp. 1438-1442; printed pp. 1415-1419): a bandlimited function can be represented in PSWF, spherical-Bessel, or sinc bases; the leading PSWFs are the unique modes that maximize energy concentration in the chosen finite interval.

Appendix B.7 (physical PDF pp. 1442-1455; printed pp. 1419-1432): PSWF expansion coefficients are obtained as eigenvectors of a symmetric tridiagonal matrix, enabling stable computation and explicit experiments in bandlimited delta approximation and superoscillation.
pedagogy: This final shard treats DSP as a transferable optimization language. It begins with elementary EMA recursions, derives their statistical, state-space, and local-polynomial meanings, then reuses the same lag, NRR, moment, least-squares, and regularization ideas in financial indicators, trend/seasonal decomposition, sparse inverse problems, neural networks, and PSWF restoration. The dominant teaching pattern is derivation followed immediately by executable MATLAB-like code and a plotted experiment. Chapter 25 is deliberately application-facing and names real trading indicators, but it also exposes their filter structures and failure modes rather than presenting them as black boxes. Chapters 26–27 are mathematically denser: learners must be comfortable with matrix least squares, quadratic forms, transforms, stochastic models, optimization, and sparse linear algebra. Chapter 28 is only a compact backpropagation primer, not a modern deep-learning course; its value is the clean matrix derivation and controlled parity/time-series experiments. The appendices mix low-level C implementation with advanced functional analysis. Exercises are unevenly distributed: Chapters 24, 26, and 27 have derivation/programming problems, Chapter 25 culminates in a long six-part Markowitz project, Chapter 28 relies on computer experiments, and Appendix A adds implementation exercises. Many historical code and data URLs need modernization, but the examples remain unusually reproducible because parameter values, datasets, and complete computational steps are given.

gems: Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1186-1188; printed pp. 1163-1165): the running mean and EMA differ by only their gain schedule—one tends to zero and becomes unable to follow regime change, while the other stays finite and deliberately sacrifices consistency for tracking.

Example 24.5.1 (physical PDF pp. 1202-1204; printed pp. 1179-1181): a d=1 EMA and equivalent zero-lag FIR follow a noiseless piecewise-linear signal almost perfectly, then the same plots reveal their very different behavior after white noise is added.

Example 24.10.1 (physical PDF pp. 1218-1219; printed pp. 1195-1196): double EMA with lambda=0.8 and 0.9 develops peaks at periods of 42 and 86 samples, a concrete warning that a causal zero-lag smoother can amplify slow oscillations.

Sec. 25.3 (physical PDF pp. 1235-1237; printed pp. 1212-1214): SMA and linearly weighted WMA are not ad hoc formulas; both fall out of the same optimum predictive-filter family at two negative prediction distances.

Sec. 25.7 (physical PDF pp. 1253-1254; printed pp. 1230-1231): on the same 20-day Nicor Gas record, the SMA lag is 9.5 days while order-2 and order-3 Butterworth smoothers have lags 4.46 and 6.31 days, making structure-versus-delay tangible.

Secs. 25.9-25.10 (physical PDF pp. 1260-1265; printed pp. 1237-1242): the text places the familiar trader's zigzag beside L0 sparse trend filtering, then explicitly warns that extrapolating the last leg is risky because a future point can turn the endpoint into a kink.

Sec. 25.11 parabolic SAR example (physical PDF pp. 1270-1274; printed pp. 1247-1251): exact reversal days 9, 15, and 27 show the candidate stop, crossing event, and reset to the prior trend's extreme—an unusually clear nonlinear-state-machine case study.

Sec. 25.14 (physical PDF pp. 1282-1293; printed pp. 1259-1270): one computer project derives the efficient frontier, no-short-sale convex program, two-fund theorem, capital asset line, Sharpe ratio, security market line, CAPM, and LCMV generalization from a single quadratic form.

Example 26.2.1 (physical PDF pp. 1299-1300; printed pp. 1276-1277): monthly Easter Island–Darwin pressure differences reveal three cycles at 12, 26, and 44 months; WH smoothing and rank-6 SVD enhancement are compared against the NIST nonlinear fit in time and frequency.

Example 26.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 1304-1305; printed pp. 1281-1282): quarterly U.S. private-investment GDP from 1947–2008 is decomposed into trend and business cycle with the canonical lambda=1600 Hodrick-Prescott filter and checked against order-3 WH and rank-1 SVD alternatives.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF p. 1308; printed p. 1285): an ill-conditioned normal matrix with eigenvalues 10^-3 and 10^3 has condition number 10^6; adding lambda=10^2,10^3,10^4 cuts it to roughly 11,2,1.1 while progressively biasing the answer.

Example 26.9.1 (physical PDF pp. 1334-1337; printed pp. 1311-1314): sparse spike deconvolution gives about 26% error with L1 but only 0.52% with the L0 IRLS experiment, while ordinary inverse filtering magnifies stopband noise.

Example 26.9.2 (physical PDF pp. 1337-1341; printed pp. 1314-1318): recovering 100 nonzeros in a 2000-vector from 1000 noisy measurements yields 71.21% error for L2, 2.54% for L1, and 0.63% for L0 IRLS.

Example 27.2.2 (physical PDF pp. 1347-1349; printed pp. 1324-1326): a two-beat synthetic ECG sampled at 600 Hz is corrupted by 60 Hz harmonics and cleaned by a D=10 notch filter; its 40-dB transient lasts 732 samples, explaining the visibly delayed cleanup.

Example 27.7.2 (physical PDF pp. 1370-1374; printed pp. 1347-1351): monthly global CO2 from 1980–2009 is separated into smooth growth and annual seasonality; removing the trend makes the harmonic comb emerge clearly in the residual spectrum.

Example 27.9.2 (physical PDF pp. 1383-1385; printed pp. 1360-1362): a simplified X-11 implementation on 1980–2008 U.S. male unemployment closely reproduces the Bureau of Labor Statistics' independently published seasonally adjusted series.

Sec. 28.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 1405-1407; printed pp. 1382-1384): a 3:3:2 network learns all eight 3-bit parity patterns to outputs near 0.01/0.99; side-by-side sigmoid/tanh and pattern/epoch curves make initialization and convergence sensitivity explicit.

Sec. 28.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 1408-1411; printed pp. 1385-1388): a 4:4:1 network trains on 250 sunspot patterns and predicts the remaining 46, with the whiteness of training residuals checked through 45 autocorrelation lags.

Appendix A.3 (physical PDF pp. 1422-1426; printed pp. 1399-1403): Voss pink noise is built from held random streams at octave periods 1,2,4,...; the construction itself explains equal energy per octave and why the lowest credible frequency is fs/2^B.

Example B.1 (physical PDF pp. 1447-1449; printed pp. 1424-1426): for c=6 the Shannon number is 3.8197, and the tabulated PSWF eigenvalues fall from 0.9999, 0.9961, 0.9402, 0.6468 to 0.2073 and then rapidly toward 10^-14.

Examples B.3-B.4 (physical PDF pp. 1450-1455; printed pp. 1427-1432): a signal containing frequencies only 0–5 locally mimics a 45-cycle waveform, but coefficients on the order of tens of millions and gigantic out-of-window amplitudes expose the price of superoscillation.
